paragraphs: Natan or Rav Natan. (Natan the prophet, [II Samuel 12](https://www.sefaria.org/II_Samuel.12.1).) Abba bar Natan, [Yerushalmi Moed Katan 3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.4.4).

Rav Ada (or Acha) bar Natan, [Chullin 49a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.49a.7). Ami bar Natan—Rabbi Ami cited without further designation. Issi bar Natan, [Berakhot 62a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.62a.10).
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan, [Berakhot 42a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.42a.5).
Rav Chiyya son of Rav Natan, [Pesachim 41a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.41a.21). Yehudah bar Natan, [Berakhot 60a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.60a.18).
Rav Kahana son of Rav Natan, [Yevamot 60b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.60b.13).
Rav Mesharshiya son of Rav Natan, [Pesachim 115a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.115a.3). Rava bar Natan, [Eruvin 32b](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.32b.4)—he is Abba bar Natan.[^3]

notes.text: This is a collective list, not a single biography. The prophet Natan is a namesake. Hyman’s Rava/Abba identification remains his claim; the cited Chiyya, Kahana and Mesharshiya passages explicitly name Rav Natan as father.
This is an index of names and patronymics, not a claim that all these men share one father or identity. Natan the prophet is a separate namesake; the Rava/Abba equation remains Hyman’s.

The Yerushalmi names Rabbi Abba bar Natan in a case involving tefillin. Eruvin separately names Rava bar Natan seated with Rabbi Assi. The comparison leaves Hyman’s proposed equation attributed to him.
